sources.name: OECD/NEA ICDE project reports on common-cause failures (ten component types)
sources.covers: Counts and shares of common-cause failure events by failure mode, severity, cause, coupling factor, detection, corrective action and population size, with event rates per observation year. No CCF parameters.
sources.boundaryConvention: An ICDE event is the complete, degraded or incipient impairment of two or more components of an observed population, within two inspection periods, from a shared cause. Severity runs from complete CCF, where all exposed components fail completely, through partial CCF and CCF impaired to incipient impairment. Each report sets its component boundary in its own coding guideline, for example a heat exchanger with its chambers, shell, tubes, adjacent piping and local valves.
sources.failureCounting: Members in Canada, Czechia, Finland, France, Germany, Japan, Korea, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States code events from licensee event reports and maintenance records under the ICDE general coding guidelines. Each event is counted once with an impairment vector, root cause, coupling factor, detection method and corrective action. Tables count events, not failed components, and observation time is summed over component groups. Data are not complete for every country and period.
sources.quality: The public reports give descriptive event statistics and engineering insights. They give no CCF parameters, no demand or run time counts and no raw event records, which stay with the members. Shares here are counts over the printed or summed table total. Where a printed total or percentage disagrees with its parts, the row says so.
sources.reference: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations, ICDE project reports on heat exchangers NEA/CSNI/R(2015)11, switching devices and circuit breakers NEA/CSNI/R(2008)1, control rod drive assemblies NEA/CSNI/R(2013)4, level measurement components NEA/CSNI/R(2008)8, batteries NEA/CSNI/R(2023)8, check valves NEA/CSNI/R(2003)15, safety and relief valves NEA/CSNI/R(2020)17, motor-operated valves NEA/CSNI/R(2021)7, emergency diesel generators NEA/CSNI/R(2018)5 and centrifugal pumps NEA/CSNI/R(2013)2

sources.name: NUREG/CR-5750 (INEEL/EXT-98-00401), Rates of Initiating Events at U.S. Nuclear Power Plants: 1987 to 1995
sources.covers: Initiating event frequencies by category, plant type and plant, event counts, critical hours and criticality factors by plant and year, LOCA frequencies from Appendix J, and comparison values from the IPEs, NUREG-1150, WASH-1400 and others
sources.boundaryConvention: An initiating event is an unplanned automatic or manual reactor trip that begins while the reactor is critical and at or above the point of adding heat. Each trip gets one initial plant fault, the first event in the sequence, from 48 mutually exclusive categories under 13 headings. Functional impact categories (26 categories under 12 headings) flag every risk-significant event that can affect decay heat removal anywhere in the trip sequence. General transients are trips with no direct impact on the systems that remove decay heat.
sources.failureCounting: Events come from Licensee Event Reports of unplanned reactor trips at U.S. commercial plants from 1987 through 1995, found through the Sequence Coding and Search System, which gave 1,985 reactor trips after screening. Each LER was coded by an experienced engineer and checked by a second analyst, and LERs that describe several trips were split. Exposure is critical years of 8,760 critical hours, 499 PWR and 230 BWR critical years for 1987-1995. Rare categories such as pipe break LOCAs, reactor coolant pump seal LOCA, two or more stuck open relief valves and total loss of service water use U.S. or world-wide experience from 1969 through 1997.
sources.quality: Counts are modeled as Poisson events with a constant rate, between-plant differences, an exponential time trend, or both, chosen by statistical tests. Constant categories use a Jeffreys noninformative prior, plant variation uses empirical Bayes gamma distributions, and trend categories report the 1995 end point. Medium and large LOCA frequencies combine crack data with a conservative conditional probability of break. The report is a scan, so every value was read from the page images. The p-values and model-choice statistics of Appendix F are not imported.
sources.reference: J. P. Poloski, D. G. Marksberry, C. L. Atwood and W. J. Galyean, NUREG/CR-5750 (INEEL/EXT-98-00401), Idaho National Engineering and Environmental Laboratory for the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, February 1999

sources.name: NUREG/CR-5496 (LOOP events 1980 to 1996) and NUREG/CR-5032 (LOOP recovery time models)
sources.covers: Loss of offsite power frequencies by category and plant mode, unit and site specific frequencies and counts, recovery time distributions and model weights, cause shares and comparisons with NUREG-1032
sources.boundaryConvention: A LOSP is the simultaneous loss of electrical power to all safety buses of a unit, which requires the emergency power generators to start and supply the safety buses. Unlike NUREG-1032, losses of non-vital buses alone are not counted. Events are classed as plant-centered, grid-related or severe weather, and as occurring at power or during shutdown. An event at power is an initiating event only if the LOSP caused the trip or both came from one root cause, and events recovered in under 2 minutes are called momentary.
sources.failureCounting: Events come from licensee event reports. NUREG/CR-5496 uses 157 events from 1980 to 1996, with plant-centered frequencies per unit critical or shutdown year and grid and weather frequencies and recovery times per site. NUREG/CR-5032 uses the 63 recovery times compiled in NUREG-1032 through 1985 plus four through June 1987. Recovery time is the time until offsite power could have been restored to at least one safety bus.
sources.quality: NUREG/CR-5496 gives Jeffreys, gamma and empirical Bayes frequency distributions and lognormal recovery times fitted after averaging multi-unit events. NUREG/CR-5032 fits exponential, lognormal, gamma and Weibull recovery models by maximum likelihood and weighs them by Bayesian posterior probabilities, with small grid and weather samples. Both reports are scans, so every value was read from the page images. Hypothesis test p-values and variance components are not imported.
sources.reference: C. L. Atwood, D. L. Kelly, F. M. Marshall, D. A. Prawdzik and J. W. Stetkar, NUREG/CR-5496 (INEEL/EXT-97-00887), INEEL for the U.S. NRC, November 1998. R. L. Iman and S. C. Hora, NUREG/CR-5032 (SAND87-2428), Sandia National Laboratories for the U.S. NRC, January 1988

sources.name: NUREG/CR-4639 Vol. 5 Part 3 Rev. 1, NUCLARR hardware component failure data (December 1988 additions)
sources.covers: Lognormal medians, 95th percentiles and error factors for 631 hardware component records with failure counts and exposure, plus five rates quoted from the source documents
sources.boundaryConvention: Each record is one cell of the NUCLARR hardware taxonomy, set by component type, design, normal state and failure mode. Instrument channel records also name the measured variable as the component application. Each record flags whether the circuit and the system are included, but the file does not define the component boundaries further.
sources.failureCounting: Most failure counts carry the record type LERS (licensee event reports), and some carry OTHR, plant operating experience. Exposure is printed as total component hours or demands, or as a number of components times hours or demands per component. For some relief valves the demand count is an average number of scrams. The records cite their source documents by NUCLARR document number only.
sources.quality: NUCLARR prints a lognormal median, a 95th percentile upper tolerance and their ratio as the error factor, computed from the failure count and exposure. The printed mean is failures over exposure, not the lognormal mean, so it is kept in the method. For zero failures on demands, 100 of 107 records print a median 6.6 to 6.8 times the Jeffreys median. This file holds only the Appendix E additions of December 1988, not the earlier Appendix D records.
sources.reference: D. I. Gertman, B. G. Gilbert, W. E. Gilmore and W. J. Galyean, NUCLARR Data Manual Part 3: Hardware Component Failure Data, NUREG/CR-4639 Vol. 5 Part 3 Rev. 1 (EGG-2458), EG&G Idaho for the U.S. NRC, January 1989

sources.name: EGG-SSRE-8875, generic component failure data base for light water and liquid sodium reactor PRAs (1990)
sources.covers: Recommended failure rates for water, steam, sodium, air and electrical components, values quoted from ten other data bases, and NUCLARR and CREDO counts with exposure
sources.boundaryConvention: Valves include the body, the operator and limit or torque switches mounted on the valve. Pumps include the body, the driver and local mechanical control. Instrumentation and control circuitry, support systems such as ac or dc power, air and hydraulics, and the solenoid valve that feeds air to a pneumatic valve are excluded. The NUCLARR and CREDO source data do not always follow these boundaries.
sources.failureCounting: NUCLARR data come from 19 plant-specific PRA and reliability study sources (category 1), LER surveys and IPRD reports with estimated demands (category 2), and IEEE Std-500, NPRD-3 and WASH-1400 (category 3), all as of February 1990. CREDO counts cover sodium and NaK components at United States and Japanese liquid metal reactors and test facilities as of February 1990. Each CREDO failure record was reviewed, some failure modes were reassigned, and events that were not failures in the PRA sense were dropped.
sources.quality: NUCLARR aggregation routines give a mean and error factor per category. CREDO means come from a Bayesian update of a noninformative prior, (2n+1)/(2T) per hour and (2n+1)/(2D+2) per demand. Recommended means are rounded to 1, 3 or 5 times a power of ten with judgemental error factors (95th percentile over median) of 3, 5, 10 or 30 under an assumed lognormal, and values based on no failures are likely conservative. The report is a scan, so every value was read from the page images.
sources.reference: S. A. Eide, S. V. Chmielewski and T. D. Swantz, EGG-SSRE-8875, EG&G Idaho, Inc. for the U.S. Department of Energy, February 1990

sources.name: NUREG/CR-4550 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 (SAND86-2084), NUREG-1150 internal events methodology and generic data
sources.covers: The NUREG-1150 generic data base: initiating event frequencies, component failure rates, test and maintenance unavailabilities, non-recovery and human error probabilities, beta factors and RCP seal LOCA probabilities, with ranges from other sources
sources.boundaryConvention: Components are listed by type and failure mode, for example motor operated valve failure to operate or diesel generator failure to run. Valve and pump demand failures include both hardware faults and control circuit or circuit breaker command faults, and the comments give the split. Test and maintenance unavailability is a separate basic event. Initiating events are grouped by their effect on offsite power and the power conversion system, and LOCAs by break size.
sources.failureCounting: The ASEP values are generic values taken or adapted from earlier compilations and PRAs, mainly the NRC LER data summaries, the IREP Procedures Guide, WASH-1400, the Station Blackout Study and IEEE Std 500. The ranges from other sources were compiled from the cited references. Test and maintenance values come from a multiple regression analysis of plant answers to NUREG-0737 questions. Failure counts are printed only for a few values.
sources.quality: ASEP values are generic means with lognormal error factors, chosen by judgment from published values rather than by a formal Bayesian update. Non-recovery probabilities have maximum entropy distributions on a printed range, and human error probabilities are medians with error factors from the ASEP HRA procedure. The data years are not printed, so 1990, the report date, bounds them. The report is a scan, so every value was read from the page images.
sources.reference: D. M. Ericson Jr. (editor), T. A. Wheeler, T. T. Sype, M. T. Drouin, W. R. Cramond, A. L. Camp, K. J. Maloney and F. T. Harper, NUREG/CR-4550 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 (SAND86-2084), Sandia National Laboratories for the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, January 1990

sources.name: IAEA-TECDOC-478 (IAEA generic component reliability data base, 1988) and IAEA-TECDOC-508 (survey of ranges, 1989)
sources.covers: Generic failure rates, demand probabilities and repair times quoted record by record from 21 sources, plus TECDOC-508 per-demand conversions and WWER data base records
sources.boundaryConvention: Each record is one component type and generic failure mode from one source, under a 5 character code for component category, group and type, generic failure mode and source. Component boundaries are those of the original source and are printed only where the source defines them, otherwise the record says detail n/a. The Swedish Reliability Data Book and the NUREG LER and IPRD studies define boundaries best, while expert and PSA sources treat components as off-the-shelf items. Operating mode defaults to all and environment to normal unless the source says otherwise.
sources.failureCounting: The IAEA did not count failures but copied each source value, with any counts and exposures the source gave placed in the record comments. The sources range from U.S. licensee event reports, plant maintenance and operating records (IPRD, Surry, Oconee, Zion, Old PWR, HWR) and Swedish failure reports, to expert opinion and mixed data (WASH-1400, IEEE Std 500, NUREG/CR-2815, IREP, German Risk Study, Sizewell B). TECDOC-508 reprints these records with hourly rates of demand failure modes converted to per demand values for an assumed monthly, quarterly or daily interval, and adds records of the WWER data base.
sources.quality: Values are reproduced without reinterpretation, so the meaning of each central value and bound follows its source: medians with 5th and 95th percentiles, Bayesian means, LER rates with confidence limits, IEEE recommended values with high and low points, or means of truncated log-uniform distributions. Range ends are separate entries and never percentiles. TECDOC-508 rows that repeat a TECDOC-478 record and value are not imported twice. Both documents are scans, so every value was read from the page images.
sources.reference: B. Tomic, Component Reliability Data for Use in Probabilistic Safety Assessment, IAEA-TECDOC-478, International Atomic Energy Agency, Vienna, October 1988. B. Tomic, Survey of Ranges of Component Reliability Data for Use in Probabilistic Safety Assessment, IAEA-TECDOC-508, International Atomic Energy Agency, Vienna, June 1989

sources.name: IAEA-TECDOC-719, Defining Initiating Events for Purposes of Probabilistic Safety Assessment (1993)
sources.covers: Initiating event frequencies from about 30 PWR, BWR and WWER PSAs, a generic data base of 272 initiator records, LOCA and rare initiator estimates, transient counts, hazard and flood frequencies
sources.boundaryConvention: An initiating event is an incident that needs an automatic or operator action to bring the plant to a safe state, usually one that causes a scram above 5 to 25 percent power. Internal events are split into LOCAs by break size, transients grouped by plant response, and special common cause initiators that also degrade mitigating systems. Break size limits and transient groups differ between PSAs, so each value keeps the definition of its source study.
sources.failureCounting: Transient counts come from EPRI NP-801, EPRI NP-2230, the EG&G study NUREG/CR-3862, licensee event reports and plant records, counted per reactor-year from commercial operation. For ATWS, events at 25 to 110 percent power are also counted on their own. The database records copy the frequencies of published PSAs and name the source table and the ultimate data source.
sources.quality: Values are quoted from the source PSAs, which used one and two stage Bayesian updating, operating experience, expert opinion, fault tree analysis and pipe and valve failure rates. The document is a scan, so every imported value was read from the page images, and the two printouts of the appendix data base were checked against each other record by record. Core damage results quoted from the PSAs are not imported.
sources.reference: D. Ilberg, assisted by B. Linquist and J. Pereq, with the WWER section by A. Bareith, IAEA-TECDOC-719, International Atomic Energy Agency, Vienna, September 1993

sources.name: CREDO papers on liquid metal reactor component reliability (six ORNL conference papers, 1985 to 1992)
sources.covers: Liquid metal and water valve failure and maintenance rates, sodium valve event counts and rates, and EBR-II, FFTF and JOYO critical item shares of failure rate, unavailability and restoration time
sources.boundaryConvention: CREDO tracks only components that are liquid metal specific, exposed to liquid metal, in systems that interface with it such as cover gas or purification, or important to safety, sorted into 45 generic categories. A valve is the body, internals, operator and other mechanical parts, and the 1992 paper adds limit and torque switches and local controls. Power, air and hydraulic supplies are outside the component, and malfunctions caused from outside are secondary events. In the critical item lists the system is the set of all CREDO-tracked components at one reactor.
sources.failureCounting: Site staff at EBR-II, FFTF, the Energy Technology Engineering Center and Westinghouse test loops, JOYO and four O-arai Engineering Center test loops send engineering, operating and event records to CREDO at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Each event record is one abnormal occurrence, failures are events that end satisfactory function, and unscheduled maintenance counts every anomaly that caused a work request. Component hours combine facility hours in each operating mode with the duty factors on the engineering record. The papers use the files as they stood from 1985 to 1992, with yearly failure rates plotted for 1978 to 1986.
sources.quality: Rates are classical point estimates, events over component hours with an exponential or Poisson model, and only the 1992 valve paper gives chi-square confidence limits. Critical item lists print only event counts and percent shares, so shares here are counts over the site event totals printed in each paper, and these totals differ between papers. Failures on demand are not separated from failures in operation, and the maintenance data mix restoration times at EBR-II and FFTF with repair times at JOYO. All six papers are scans, so every value was read from the page images.
sources.reference: S. L. Painter, H. E. Knee and B. Humphrys, CONF-850713-4, July 1985. M. J. Haire, H. E. Knee, J. J. Manning, J. F. Manneschmidt and K. Setoguchi, CONF-870468-1, April 1987. B. L. Humphrys, M. J. Haire, K. H. Koger, J. F. Manneschmidt, K. Setoguchi, R. Nakai and Y. Okubo, CONF-870917-2, September 1987. K. H. Koger, M. J. Haire, B. L. Humphrys, J. F. Manneschmidt, K. Setoguchi and R. Nakai, CONF-880601-34, June 1988. D. H. Wood, M. S. Smith and J. D. Drischler, CONF-920818-2, August 1992. M. S. Smith and J. D. Drischler, CONF-930116-8, 1992. Oak Ridge National Laboratory, with the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation of Japan for the 1987 and 1988 papers.

sources.name: ANL-NSE-2, EBR-II Level 1 Probabilistic Risk Assessment (Argonne, 1991 final draft, published 2018)
sources.covers: EBR-II initiating event frequencies and counts, basic event failure rates and demand probabilities with CRBRP-4, IREP and generic comparison values, beta and MGL factors, human error probabilities, external event frequencies and refueling data for a sodium cooled pool reactor
sources.boundaryConvention: Each basic event is one component and one failure mode in a system fault tree, named by an eight character code, and wiring, fuses, relay coils and contacts are separate basic events. Initiating events are grouped by plant response, such as single and double primary pump loss of flow, reactivity insertions, loss of heat sink and local faults. Each human failure event is one task quantified with a human event tree. Models reflect the plant as of October 1989 with three 100 day runs per year.
sources.failureCounting: Initiating event counts come from EBR-II Unusual Occurrence Reports for 1975 to 1989, and rare events use fault trees or engineering judgment. Component values start from IEEE Std 500, IREP and the Clinch River Breeder Reactor PRA (CRBRP-4) and are refined with CREDO data checked against EBR-II records. For the reactor shutdown system a plant record survey counted unsafe failures against 1.80E+5 hours per component. Human error probabilities come from the NUREG/CR-1278 and NUREG/CR-4772 tables.
sources.quality: Basic event values are lognormal means with the listed error factors, and plant specific rates use the mean (2N+1)/(2T) of a noninformative prior update. Common cause uses generic beta factors because EBR-II had almost no common cause events, and many values rest on engineering judgment. The seismic section is a placeholder and two pages of Section 10 are missing from the scan. All values were read from the page images, and physics tables and sequence results are not imported.
sources.reference: D. J. Hill, W. A. Ragland and J. Roglans-Ribas, Experimental Breeder Reactor II (EBR-II) Level 1 Probabilistic Risk Assessment, ANL-NSE-2, Argonne National Laboratory, final draft June 30, 1991, published August 1, 2018

sources.name: MIL-HDBK-217F Notice 2, Reliability Prediction of Electronic Equipment
sources.covers: Part stress base failure rates and pi factors for electronic parts, plus parts count generic failure rates by environment and quality factors
sources.boundaryConvention: Most part types have a model in which a base failure rate is multiplied by pi factors for environment, quality, temperature, electrical stress, application and construction, and microcircuit models add die and package terms. The part models include catastrophic and permanent drift failures, while failures from connecting parts into assemblies are counted in the interconnection assembly and connection sections. Fourteen use environments run from ground benign to cannon launch, and no model covers ionizing radiation.
sources.failureCounting: The handbook prints model parameters and tables of calculated values, not failure counts or exposure. The models rest on the best data available when each section was issued, and Notice 2 revised the resistor, capacitor, inductive, rotating, relay, switch, connector, circuit board and connection models from a newer study. Rates are printed in failures per 10^6 hours and stored per hour.
sources.quality: Base rates and factors are point estimates with no uncertainty bounds, and all parts except motors are taken to have a constant failure rate. The handbook warns that a prediction is not the field reliability users will measure. The copy is a scan, so every imported table page was read as an image and checked against its printed equation. The superseded MIL-HDBK-217E pages bundled in the same file are not imported.
sources.reference: U.S. Department of Defense, MIL-HDBK-217F, Reliability Prediction of Electronic Equipment, 2 December 1991, with Notice 1 (10 July 1992) and Notice 2 (28 February 1995), preparing activity Rome Laboratory

sources.name: NSWC-11 Handbook of Reliability Prediction Procedures for Mechanical Equipment (May 2011)
sources.covers: Base failure rates and tabulated correction factors of mechanical part models, plus sensing element and miscellaneous part rates
sources.boundaryConvention: Each component is modeled as the sum of its parts, such as seals, springs, bearings, housings and fluid drivers, and each part has its own model. A base failure rate covers the part at reference conditions and multiplying factors adjust it to the actual design and operating environment. Part failure is defined by function, for example leakage above an allowable rate for seals and valves or wear-out of friction material.
sources.failureCounting: Base rates are normalized to field data such as the Navy Maintenance and Material Management (3-M) system, published data bases such as NPRD-95 and OREDA, maker life data and laboratory tests. The handbook prints no failure counts or exposure for these rates. Only the valve validation test table gives cycles to failure for single test valves.
sources.quality: Values are point estimates from engineering models that combine physics of failure equations with normalization to field data, without uncertainty bounds. The handbook calls itself a research product with limited validation testing. Factors given only as equations or curves sit in the method of the related base rate row.
sources.reference: Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock Division, Handbook of Reliability Prediction Procedures for Mechanical Equipment, CARDEROCKDIV NSWC-11, West Bethesda, Maryland, May 2011

elicitations.outsideReason: No one on the PRA team has operated a passive cavity cooling system. The uncertainty is large and the system is risk significant (4.2.3 d).

parameters.name: Protection division trip logic fails to trip

sourceUses.reason: A bistable that fails to trip is the main failure of a trip division. The INL row covers the bistable alone, so a factor adds the rest of the division.

factors.name: Process logic and trip relays in the division
factors.basis: Adding PLP-FTOP (1.6E-4) and two RLY-FTOP (2.5E-5 each) to BIS-FTOP (5.4E-4) gives 1.4 times the bistable alone.

sourceUses.reason: Already counted in the division factor on BIS-FTOP.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. The trip divisions use the bistable, logic and relay technology that the LWR protection system studies cover.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A standby component asked to change state, estimated per demand.

parameters.name: Control rods fail to insert

sourceUses.reason: The elicitation addressed exactly this event, one division's rods failing to insert after the trip signal.
A single PWR rod inserted by its own drive. A division fails only if its group of reflector rods does not insert.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. No data source covers gravity insertion of reflector rods. The LWR rows count single rods of another design.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A standby component asked to change state, estimated per demand.

parameters.name: Shutdown-cooling circulator fails to run

sourceUses.reason: A motor-driven compressor running past its first hour is the closest industry machine to an electric helium circulator. Both boundaries hold the driver, local breaker and local cooling.

factors.name: Helium service with a sealed motor and magnetic bearings
factors.basis: Sealed helium machines add bearing control and seal systems that air compressors lack.

sourceUses.reason: Helium circulators in gas-cooled reactor service. Their steam and water turbine drives and water bearings differ, so the count enters Step 05 as evidence, not as the prior.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. Fort St. Vrain is the only helium circulator record from a power reactor.
parameters.priorFormReason: The compressor row comes from 90 failures in 1.6 million hours, so it is very narrow, and scaling it by 2 keeps that narrowness although the factor runs from 1 to 5. As published it conflicts with the Fort St. Vrain counts (P = 2.6E-9). The constrained noninformative form keeps its mean and lets the helium circulator experience speak.
parameters.estimateReason: The estimate is about twelve times lower than the compressor prior. Fort St. Vrain ran 253,886 machine hours with two failures the design shares, so the helium circulator experience outweighs the air compressor prior. The published prior stays as sensitivity case SS-2.

evidence.label: Fort St. Vrain circulators
evidence.reason: Five helium circulators of the only U.S. gas-cooled power reactor. They share the helium compressor, shaft and internals with the design's circulator. Incidents in the steam and water drives, water bearings and seals are judged against the design's boundary in RS-01. The exposure is the 253,886 combined machine hours of Figure 4, steam plus water drive.

parameters.multiPosApplicabilityJustification: Applies across POS-01 to POS-07 and POS-09, with applicability verified for each state before reuse.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A running failure over the 24 h mission, carried as a per-mission probability.

parameters.name: Shutdown cooler fouled

sourceUses.reason: Plugging or loss of heat transfer of a shell and tube heat exchanger. The cooler's water side fouls by the same mechanisms.
Chemical process and gas service, thirty times the nuclear fleet value. The cooler sees clean water.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. No HTGR heat exchanger fouling record exists, so industry heat exchangers in clean cooling-water service are the closest population.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A running failure over the 24 h mission, carried as a per-mission probability.

parameters.name: Cavity-cooling duct group blocked

sourceUses.reason: Duct plugging per foot of duct in DOE ventilation systems. Scaled by the length of one duct group and by its exposure to outside air.

factors.name: Duct length per group, in feet
factors.basis: One riser with its inlet and outlet runs, about 120 m in all.

factors.name: Open-air intake exposed to debris, snow and nesting
factors.basis: The source ducts carry filtered building air. The cavity cooling intakes face weather and animals.

sourceUses.reason: The panel judged blockage of one air path over the mission. Kept as the comparison case for the scaled duct data.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. No cavity cooling system has operated at power. Duct plugging data from DOE facilities are the closest measured population.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A running failure over the 72 h mission, carried as a per-mission probability.

parameters.name: Common exhaust stack blocked

sourceUses.reason: The panel judged blockage of one air path, the stack included, over the 72 h mission.
A single large stack does not plug like a duct run. Blocking it takes a structural collapse or massive debris.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. No source records the failure of a large exhaust stack, and duct plugging data do not describe one.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A running failure over the 72 h mission, carried as a per-mission probability.

parameters.name: Steam-generator isolation valve fails to close

sourceUses.reason: Large steam isolation valves with their operators, local breakers and controls. The row pools failures to open and to close, so it bounds failure to close.
General motor-operated valves, a lower comparison case for failure to close.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. The steam and feedwater isolation valves match LWR main steam isolation service.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A standby component asked to change state, estimated per demand.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation.

sourceUses.reason: The trip unit of a detection channel. A factor adds the detector and its signal path.

factors.name: Detector and signal path ahead of the trip unit
factors.basis: A pressure transmitter on demand (STP-FTOP-D, 1.2E-4) adds about a fifth. Gas leak detectors are less proven, so the factor runs to 3.

parameters.evidenceReason: There are no plant records before operation. The leak detection channels use the sensing and trip technology of the LWR protection studies.
parameters.modelSelectionBasis: A standby component asked to change state, estimated per demand.

restoration.subject: Offsite power
restoration.windowReason: Shutdown cooling must start within 33 h of the loss of forced cooling (SY DU-SCS-1, and HR-POST-018 allows 1,980 min). Offsite power back inside that time restores shutdown cooling.
restoration.sequence: POS-01 full power, loss of offsite power (IE-06) leading to the station-blackout family EFQ-4 in ESF-LATE
restoration.basis: Generic offsite power recovery data, as the standard asks before operation (DA-C23). The four LOOP categories are weighted by their critical-operation frequencies. The LOOP 2023 update is the estimate. The NUREG/CR-6890 fits give about a third of it, because the newer data recover more slowly in every category, most of all for plant-centered and weather-related losses.

parameters.modelSelectionBasis: Probability that the restoration takes longer than the time available in the sequence.

parameters.name: Shutdown cooling not restarted from the remote panel in time

sourceUses.reason: The panel judged the restart time for this panel and this train design.

parameters.evidenceReason: No restart has been timed on the panel yet. Simulator timing replaces the judgment once the panel exists.

restoration.subject: Shutdown-cooling restart from the remote panel
restoration.windowReason: HR-POST-018 allows 1,980 min in POS-07. Less the 10 min cue and the 30 min first attempt, about 32 h remain for the remote-panel restart.
restoration.sequence: POS-07 post-trip passive cooling, sequence family ESF-LATE, recovery REC-1
restoration.basis: Supports the Human Reliability recovery credit REC-Q-1. The restart time is far inside the window, so the credit rests on the operator action itself.

parameters.modelSelectionBasis: Probability that the restoration takes longer than the time available in the sequence.

parameters.name: Backup gas-turbine generator not repaired within the shutdown-cooling start window

sourceUses.reason: Repair times of the easier of two failed diesel generators from US plant unplanned outage data. The gas turbines share the generator, breaker and control scope, but the prime mover differs.

parameters.evidenceReason: No plant repair records exist before operation (DA-C21).

restoration.subject: Backup gas-turbine generator
restoration.windowReason: The same 33 h shutdown-cooling start window as offsite power recovery (SY DU-SCS-1).
restoration.sequence: POS-01 full power, loss of offsite power with both backup generators failed, family EFQ-4 in ESF-LATE
restoration.basis: Systems Analysis credits no repair yet (SY-A31), so the curve is ready for when it does. Repair time runs from finding the failure to return to service (DA-C20).

parameters.modelSelectionBasis: Probability that the restoration takes longer than the time available in the sequence.

failureModes.name: Fails to start
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A standby component does not start or change state when demanded.

failureModes.name: Fails to run
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A running component stops before the mission time ends.

failureModes.name: Fails to load and run
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A standby generator starts but fails to pick up its loads or stops in its first hour of running.

failureModes.name: Fails to open
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A closed valve, damper or breaker does not open on demand.

failureModes.name: Fails to close
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: An open valve or damper does not close on demand.

failureModes.name: Fails to trip
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: Protection logic does not generate the trip at its setpoint.

failureModes.name: Plugged or fouled
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A flow path, duct or heat-transfer surface is blocked or fouled.

failureModes.name: Fails to operate
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: An instrument, detector or alarm does not respond on demand.

failureModes.name: Unavailable
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A standby supply is not available when demanded.

failureModes.name: Faults in operation
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A running component develops a fault that defeats its function.

failureModes.name: Fails to insert
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: Control rods do not enter the core after release.

failureModes.name: Spurious operation
failureModes.mechanismOfFailure: A component changes state without a demand.

failureEventClassifications.failureDefinitionBasis: A component state is a failure when it cannot perform its modeled function on demand or over its mission.
degradedStatesCountedAsFailures: Circulator fails to reach rated speed
Damper opens but does not reach the full-open stop
Charger output below the float band
degradedStatesNotCounted: Slow damper stroke that still completes within the allowed time
Cosmetic seal weep with the function intact

failureEventClassifications.failureDefinitionBasis: The circulator fails to run when it stops, or must be stopped, while shutdown cooling needs it. A part found damaged at a planned removal counts only if the damage would have ended a run.
degradedStatesCountedAsFailures: Trip or forced shutdown of a running machine
Damage that would have stopped the rotor during the mission
degradedStatesNotCounted: Static shutdown seal faults, since the seal acts only at standstill
Planned surveillance removals that find no defect
Faults in parts the design does not have, such as water turbines and water-lubricated bearings

recordSets.name: Fort St. Vrain helium circulator incidents
recordSets.reference: H. L. Brey, Fort St. Vrain circulator operating experience, Public Service Company of Colorado, OSTI ETDE 7955681, Table 2 and Figure 4

records.description: Pre-nuclear water turbine (Pelton wheel) cavitation in hot functional testing. Two machines lost buckets.
records.reason: The water turbine backup drive is outside the design's boundary, which has an electric motor and no water turbine. The damage came in pre-nuclear testing with oversized wheels.
The bearing water auxiliary is outside the circulator boundary, and the design's magnetic bearings use no water.

records.description: Static shutdown seal inner bellows ruptured from an overpressure. Pressure control improved.
records.reason: The static shutdown seal is applied only after the brake stops the rotor, so its failure cannot stop a running machine.

records.description: Fatigue cracks in the water turbine buckets and the curvic coupling. Wrought wheels installed.
records.reason: The water turbine drive is outside the design's boundary. The cracks were also self-arresting and would not have impaired the circulator.

records.description: Static shutdown seal face leak. Brake sequencing control improved.
records.reason: The seal was actuated while the rotor turned, a sequencing fault. The static seal plays no part in running.

records.description: Static shutdown seal supply line leak. Repaired to drawing.
records.reason: A leak in the static seal's supply line does not stop a running machine.

records.description: Static shutdown seal bellows crack from overextension before installation. Seal qualification test changed.
records.reason: A static seal fault found with the machine idle. Running was not affected.

records.description: Primary seal leak. Bolt material, thread form and torque changed on all machines.
records.reason: The primary seal keeps bearing water and buffer helium out of the primary coolant. A sealed motor with magnetic bearings has no such seal.
A planned surveillance removal. The inspection found no abnormal wear or degradation.

records.description: Static shutdown seal outer bellows crack from a forming-tool groove, found at very low power.
records.reason: An isolated manufacturing defect of the static seal. Running was not affected.

records.description: Static shutdown seal bellows leak. Design modification made.
records.reason: A static seal fault. Running was not affected.
The discharge valve sits outside the circulator boundary.

records.description: Bearing water line leak from a bolt manufacturing defect.
records.reason: The design's magnetic bearings have no water lines.

records.description: Stress corrosion of the compressor end bolts, found from January to June 1985. Bolt material changed.
records.reason: Cracked compressor end bolts could end a run, and the compressor end is common to both designs. One cause on all machines counts once (DA-C6).

records.description: Circulator trip at about 70% power. The insulation shield and labyrinth seal failed and dropped onto the steam turbine wheel.
records.reason: A running machine tripped when an internal part failed. The design's internals are not yet proven against this, so it counts.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: RPS trip divisions
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The design surveillance plan tests the trip channels of the two divisions on separate schedules, as the Systems Analysis group records. Each division is tested alone, so the testing is staggered.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The CCF 2020 data have no template for trip logic divisions. The report advises its generic demand factors when no component template fits, and a division fails on a trip demand.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The division boundary (CB-5) holds the trip logic channel and its power supply, with the rod release outside. The generic factors pool many component types, so they carry no single boundary to match.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Control-rod insertion
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The design calls for periodic rod-drop timing tests but gives no stagger between the divisions. Non-staggered is the conservative choice when the scheme is not known.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The CCF 2020 data have no template for control rod drives. The generic demand factors apply because the rods fail to insert on a trip demand.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: Each group's boundary (CB-6) holds the drive, its release latch and the rods, with the trip logic outside. The generic factors pool many component types, so they carry no single boundary to match.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Backup gas-turbine generators
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The Systems Analysis group records staggered start testing. Each generator is started alone on its own schedule.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: No gas-turbine generator template exists. The emergency diesel generator fail-to-start factors are the closest standby generator data. Both kinds start from standby on demand with their own starting systems.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The generator boundary (CB-20) holds the turbine, generator, starting system and skids. The diesel generator events also count the generator breaker, which the model carries as its own event without a common cause group, so breaker shared causes are counted once, inside these factors.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Shutdown-cooling trains
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The design surveillance plan tests the trains in turn so one stays available, as the train maintenance events in Systems Analysis record. That is staggered testing.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The circulator's independent prior is the motor-driven compressor running past its first hour (Step 04). The compressor fail-to-run factors keep the same component and failure mode.

evidence.label: Fort St. Vrain circulators

events.description: Stress corrosion of the compressor end bolts on all machines
events.reason: One cause was found on all four machines, so both members of any pair fail together. The compressor end is common to both designs, and Step 05 counts the record as one failure.

events.description: Water turbine cavitation on all machines in hot functional testing
events.reason: The water turbine drive is outside the design's boundary. Step 05 leaves the record out for the same reason (DA-D9).

events.description: Fatigue cracks in the water turbine buckets on all machines
events.reason: The water turbine drive is outside the design's boundary, and the cracks would not have stopped a machine. Step 05 leaves the record out too (DA-D9).

evidence.reason: Fort St. Vrain ran four helium circulators at a time, the same component in the same helium service. R-15 is the one counted failure of a single machine, so it is the independent count. A group of two takes 1 × 2 / 4 = 0.5 of it.

ccfParameterEstimations.estimateReason: The compressor factors hold few shared-cause events, so the one Fort St. Vrain event moves the pair term by about two thirds. Helium circulator experience is the closer evidence, so the update stands.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The train boundary (CB-1) holds the circulator, motor, local breaker and train control circuit, like the compressor template. Fort St. Vrain's steam and water drives differ, so its events are judged against the design boundary record by record.
ccfParameterEstimations.genericExclusionConsistencyBasis: Each Fort St. Vrain record carries one judgment, made in Step 05. R-14 counts as a failure there and as a shared-cause event here. R-01 and R-04 are outside the boundary in both. The other records involve one machine and no shared cause.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Class-1E station batteries
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The Systems Analysis group staggers the equalizing charges, but they are maintenance and reveal no failed bank. No staggered battery test is documented, so the conservative non-staggered scheme applies.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: Station batteries of the same kind. The fail-to-operate factors cover a bank that cannot carry its load, the members' failure mode.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The bank boundary (CB-4) holds the cells, rack and DC bus disconnect, with the charger outside. That matches the battery events, which code charger faults to the charger.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Cavity cooling duct groups
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: No staggered inspection of the duct groups is documented. Non-staggered is the conservative choice when the scheme is not known.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: No CCF 2020 template covers air ducts or passive cooling paths. The generic rate factors pool failures that build up over time, like plugging between inspections. Strainer and screen plugging data exist, but they come from raw-water debris and fouling, not dust in air ducts.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: Each duct group's boundary (CB-2) holds the riser, intake screen, damper and position switch. The generic factors pool many component types, so they carry no single boundary to match.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Steam-generator isolation valves
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: Both valves follow one test procedure, as the Systems Analysis group records, so they are tested together. That is non-staggered testing.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The isolation valves close a steam line on demand, the duty of a PWR main steam isolation valve.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The valve boundary (CB-9) holds the body, operator, local breaker and local controls, the industry valve boundary that the main steam valve events use.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Cooling-water pumps
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: The pumps alternate lead and lag in service, and running time reveals their failures. No staggered test is documented, so the conservative non-staggered scheme applies.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: Component cooling water motor-driven pumps that fail to run, the members' type, service and failure mode.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The pump boundary (CB-23) holds the pump, motor, local breaker, lubrication, cooling and controls, the industry motor-driven pump boundary.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Moisture monitors
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: No staggered test of the two monitors is documented. Non-staggered is the conservative choice when the scheme is not known.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The CCF 2020 data have no template for moisture analyzers or other process instruments. The generic demand factors apply because a monitor fails when the isolation signal demands it.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The monitor boundary (CB-25) holds the sampler, analyzer and trip output. No industry component matches it, so the generic factors are used without a boundary match, the same open item as the independent estimate.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Helium boundary isolation valves
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: Both valves follow one test procedure, as the Systems Analysis group records, so they are tested together. That is non-staggered testing.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: Motor-operated isolation valves that must close on demand, the members' type and failure mode.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The valve boundary (CB-12) holds the body, operator, local breaker and local controls, the industry valve boundary.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Primary pressure channels
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: Each channel is calibrated on its own, but no stagger between the channels is documented. Non-staggered is the conservative choice when the scheme is not known.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: The CCF 2020 data have no pressure transmitter template. The generic demand factors apply because a channel fails when the alarm demands it.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The channel boundary (CB-13) holds the sensor, transmitter and signal card. The generic factors pool many component types, so they carry no single boundary to match.

ccfParameterEstimations.name: Building isolation dampers
ccfParameterEstimations.testingReason: Both dampers follow one test procedure, as the Systems Analysis group records, so they are tested together. That is non-staggered testing.
ccfParameterEstimations.priorReason: No damper template exists. Air-operated valves that fail to close are the closest data, since the dampers are air-operated and must close on demand.
ccfParameterEstimations.componentBoundaryConsistencyBasis: The damper boundary (CB-18) holds the blades, operator, local controls and position switch, which matches an air-operated valve with its operator.

dataModificationAdjustments.modificationDescription: Fort St. Vrain compressor end bolts changed to a new material after stress corrosion cracking
dataModificationAdjustments.basis: R-14 stays counted. The design's own compressor bolting is not yet proven against this mechanism.

dataModificationAdjustments.modificationDescription: Fort St. Vrain water turbine wheels replaced by wrought wheels, with water turbine speed limited to 7000 rpm
dataModificationAdjustments.basis: Both water turbine incidents, R-01 and R-04, are left out as outside the boundary, so the change does not touch the counted failures.

uncertaintyRegister.source: Similar-equipment adjustment for the moisture monitors
uncertaintyRegister.impact: The monitors take nonnuclear moisture-analyzer data adjusted for sampling helium at pressure. Over the factor's range the monitor probability runs from 1.80E-3 to 1.08E-2.
uncertaintyRegister.assumption: Nonnuclear moisture analyzers fail like the helium moisture monitors once the sampling factor is applied.
uncertaintyRegister.assumptionBasis: The sensing cell and electronics are the same. Only the sample conditioning differs.

alternatives.alternative: Pool wider nonnuclear experience for the sparse failure modes.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: Applicability could not be established beyond the moisture-monitor adjustment.

uncertaintyRegister.source: Fort St. Vrain circulator incidents and the circulator prior
uncertaintyRegister.impact: Two of fifteen incidents count. Counting every removal would raise the circulator rate about six times, and the published compressor prior would raise it 9.2 times.

alternatives.alternative: Count every circulator removal as a failure.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: Most removals were inspections and external problems outside the design's boundary.

alternatives.alternative: Use the published compressor prior as it is.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: It conflicts with the Fort St. Vrain counts, so its mean is kept in a constrained noninformative prior.

uncertaintyRegister.keyReason: The circulator sits in the shutdown-cooling common cause group, the highest-ranked item in ESQ, and its rate moves several times with the judgment and the prior.

uncertaintyRegister.source: Planned demand, exposure and maintenance counts
uncertaintyRegister.impact: Demands, run hours and maintenance hours come from the planned schedule until operating records exist. Each train unavailability moves in proportion to its maintenance hours.
uncertaintyRegister.assumption: The planned surveillance and maintenance schedule stands in for operating records.

alternatives.alternative: Use plant records for demands, exposure and failures once operating.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: No operating records exist yet at the pre-operational stage.

uncertaintyRegister.impact: The joint equalizing charge takes both battery banks out together for 22 h a year. The value is assumed until plant experience confirms it.

alternatives.alternative: Stagger the equalizing charges so only one bank is out at a time.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: The design maintenance plan charges both banks together. Staggering is left to the operating procedures.

uncertaintyRegister.source: Initiating-event frequencies for a design with no operating history
uncertaintyRegister.impact: Twenty-one group frequencies rest on IE fault trees, generic data and design-based estimates. At the 2020 industry rates loss of offsite power would drop 2.8 times.

alternatives.alternative: Estimate loss of offsite power from the 2020 industry rates alone.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: The IE group also holds loss of the plant's normal AC distribution, which the industry offsite power rates do not count.

uncertaintyRegister.keyReason: Each group frequency scales its sequence frequencies directly.

uncertaintyRegister.source: Common cause factors from the CCF 2020 data
uncertaintyRegister.impact: Each group takes generic factors for its size, and its testing scheme decides what Systems Analysis receives. Testing the shutdown-cooling trains on one day would make both failing together 2.0 times more likely.

alternatives.alternative: Use common cause data from gas-cooled plants.
alternatives.reasonNotSelected: Fort St. Vrain gives one shared-cause circulator event, too few for factors beyond the circulator pair.

uncertaintyRegister.keyReason: The shutdown-cooling train common cause group has the highest importance in ESQ.

sensitivityCases.name: Similar-equipment sweep
sensitivityCases.reason: The moisture monitors rest on nonnuclear moisture analyzers. Their sampling factor goes to its bounds of 0.5 and 3.
sensitivityCases.results: The monitor probability runs from 1.80E-3 to 1.08E-2 per demand, against 3.60E-3 for the nominal factor.

sensitivityCases.name: Prior-form comparison
sensitivityCases.reason: The circulator update repeated with the published compressor prior in place of the constrained noninformative one.
sensitivityCases.results: With the published prior the 24 h circulator probability is 2.13E-3, 9.2 times the 2.32E-4 of the base case. The published prior conflicts with the Fort St. Vrain counts, so it stays a sensitivity case.

sensitivityCases.name: Train maintenance sweep
sensitivityCases.reason: Shutdown-cooling train maintenance between half and twice the planned 35 h a year.
sensitivityCases.results: The train unavailability runs from 2.00E-3 to 7.99E-3, against 4.00E-3 for the plan.

sensitivityCases.name: Coincident-maintenance sweep
sensitivityCases.reason: The joint battery equalization unavailability from none to 5.0E-3.
sensitivityCases.results: The planned joint charge gives 2.51E-3, inside the swept range.

sensitivityCases.name: Offsite power at the 2020 rates
sensitivityCases.reason: Loss of offsite power at the 2020 industry rates, power and shutdown, against the IE group that also holds loss of normal AC.
sensitivityCases.results: The 2020 rates give 3.42E-2 per year over the group's states, 2.8 times below the IE group frequency of 9.75E-2.

sensitivityCases.name: Shutdown-cooling testing scheme
sensitivityCases.reason: The two shutdown-cooling trains tested on one day instead of staggered.
sensitivityCases.results: Both trains failing together rises from 1.69E-6 to 3.35E-6, 2.0 times the staggered value.

documentation.processDescription: Parameters defined, grouped, collected, estimated and documented by a systematic process, per ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4 HLR-DA-A through E, with each number carrying a pedigree on the evidence ladder.
documentation.systemComponentBoundaries: Each component boundary, failure mode and success criterion is matched to the Systems Analysis basic-event definition, so the model boundary and the data boundary agree.
documentation.basicEventProbabilityModels: Each basic event carries a probability model that fits how it is demanded, a demand probability for components asked to start and a failure rate for components failing over time.
documentation.genericParameterSources: Generic estimates are collected from recognized industry sources per operating state, with applicable experience from other facilities including nonnuclear ones at the pre-operational stage.
documentation.plantSpecificDataSourcesAndPeriods: The plant is pre-operational and has no records, so plant-specific collection is replaced by disciplined borrowing with the applicability recorded.
documentation.dataExclusionJustifications: Any exclusion of data from the collection is justified, and an event excluded from the independent database is excluded from the common-cause database too.
documentation.demandAndExposureCounting: Demands are estimated from the planned surveillance and maintenance schedule, and exposure hours from the planned test practices, since no operating records exist.
documentation.unavailabilityTreatment: Only activities that disable the function are counted, and an unavailability caused by a support system is assigned to that support system so the dependency is not buried.
documentation.repairAndRecoveryData: Repair time runs from identification of the failure to restoration, and recovery times for offsite power, component cooling water and the shutdown-cooling function are taken from generic sources.
documentation.lpsdOutageData: Outage timelines and counts per calendar year are collected as the raw material behind the POS time fractions and the initiating-event frequencies.
documentation.componentGroupingAndOutliers: Components are pooled into homogeneous groups by type and service, with outliers such as a mothballed spare and a test rig held out of the pools.
documentation.ccfParameterBasis: Common cause factors come from the CCF 2020 alpha-factor data for each group's size. Each group records its testing scheme. Staggered groups pass MGL values to Systems Analysis and the rest pass alpha factors, so each combination matches the scheme. The circulator pair is updated with the one Fort St. Vrain shared-cause event.
documentation.bayesianPriorRationales: Each estimate starts from the prior chosen in Step 04. The circulator prior keeps the compressor mean in a constrained noninformative form, because the published form conflicts with the Fort St. Vrain evidence. Each update is checked against its prior.
documentation.parameterEstimatesWithUncertainty: Point estimates with uncertainty are provided at CC-I and realistic mean estimates for risk-significant events at CC-II, each with a characterized distribution.
documentation.multiPosGenericUse: The applicability of a generic estimate to each operating state is established before the estimate is reused across states.
documentation.modelUncertaintySources: The register holds six sources: the moisture-monitor adjustment, the Fort St. Vrain circulator judgment and prior, the planned counts, the coincident maintenance, the initiating-event frequencies and the CCF 2020 factors. Each has a sensitivity case.
documentation.asBuiltLimitations: Pre-operational: boundaries, counts, priors and assumed values rest on design and planning information pending as-built and as-operated confirmation.
documentation.praTaskInterfaces: DA takes the basic-event list from SY and the outage timelines from POS, and supplies failure rates, demand probabilities, unavailabilities and CCF parameters to IE, SY and HR, with everything converging on ESQ.

comments.text: The battery charger boundary CB-3 may overlap the battery basic event, so DA-A2 needs the boundary reconciled with the Systems Analysis before the charger parameter is used.
The sodium check-valve parameter is adjusted from a water valve, so DA-D2 needs the adjustment basis documented and bounded by a sensitivity study.
comments.resolution: The adjustment is documented on the check-valve parameter and bounded by the similar-equipment sweep SS-1.

comments.text: The sensor input module estimate updates a Savannah River prior with EBR-II shutdown-system experience, so DA-D5 needs the relative weight of prior versus evidence shown to be reasonable.
comments.resolution: The EBR-II hours equal about 890 quarterly test intervals with no failure. The evidence agrees with the prior (P = 0.76) and lowers the mean by about 13 percent.

comments.text: The pump generic estimate is reused across the standby and reduced-power states, so DA-C25 needs the applicability to each state established before reuse.
comments.resolution: The applicability per state is recorded on each generic source and on the multi-state parameters.

comments.text: The mothballed spare and the test charger are held out of the pools consistently.
comments.resolution: No change required, the outlier rule is applied consistently.

sources.name: WSRC-TR-93-262 Rev. 1, Savannah River Site generic data base (1998)
sources.covers: Recommended lognormal failure rates for about 500 water, chemical process, compressed gas, HVAC, electrical and instrument component modes, with the category 1, 2 and 3 source data and aggregated results behind them
sources.boundaryConvention: Components and failure modes follow a Savannah River Site list in six system types: water, chemical process, compressed gas, HVAC/exhaust, electrical distribution, and instrumentation and control. Each row has an identifier made of a component code, a failure mode code and a system code (Tables 7 to 9), such as PIP-LE-W for external leakage of water piping. Pipe, hose, tube and duct rates are per hour per foot and the cable rate is per 1000 ft. Leak and rupture values taken from EGG-SSRE-9639 define rupture as a leak of more than 50 gpm.
sources.failureCounting: Category 1 sources give failure counts with reviewed populations and exposures, from nuclear power plant PRAs and Swedish plant data gathered in NUCLARR, plus Savannah River Site reactor data. Category 2 sources give actual failure data with added uncertainty, such as LER and in-plant reliability surveys of nuclear plant components, NPRD-3, OREDA, the Idaho Chemical Processing Plant (WIN-330), a tritium handling facility and an LNG plant. Category 3 sources list only failure rate estimates, from WASH-1400, the CCPS guidelines, IEEE Std 500-1984, a natural gas facility study, two EPRI power plant reports and EGG-SSRE-8875. Counts are failures over component hours or demands, and judgment was used to split failures among failure modes.
sources.quality: Within a category, data sets were pooled by matching the moments of a lognormal distribution, and sparse data used a Bayesian update of a noninformative prior with an error factor of 10. Category 3 estimates were combined by averaging lognormal parameters. The recommended value takes category 1 first, then category 2, then category 3, rounded to 1, 3 or 5 times a power of 10, and Rev. 1 limits error factors to 10. The data years are not printed, so 1998, the Rev. 1 date, bounds them. The report is a scan, so every value was read from the page images.
sources.reference: A. Blanchard and B. N. Roy, Savannah River Site Generic Data Base Development, WSRC-TR-93-262 Rev. 1 (WSMSC-98-0162), Westinghouse Savannah River Company and Westinghouse Safety Management Solutions, May 1998 (original issue 1993)

sources.name: CCF Parameter Estimations, 2020 Update, Revision 1 (INL/EXT-21-62940)
sources.covers: Alpha factor distributions, MLEs and MGL parameters for CCCG sizes 2 to 8 by component, system and failure mode, plus generic and prior distributions
sources.boundaryConvention: Each CCF template is a query rule over the NRC CCF database by component type, failure mode and, where named, system or plant group. Pooled templates cover all systems. A CCF event needs two or more failed or degraded components at one plant and in one system, from a single shared cause. Failures caused by equipment outside the component boundary are excluded.
sources.failureCounting: CCF events and independent failure counts come from the NRC CCF database for 1/1/2006 to 12/31/2020, queried in RADS with the SPAR Rules 2020 folder. Each event is coded as an impact vector with degradation, timing and shared cause factors and mapped to CCCG sizes 2 to 8. Only CCF events are counted and unavailability events are excluded.
sources.quality: Each template is a Bayesian update of the 2015 generic Dirichlet prior (1997-2015 data) with the mapped impact vectors. The report prints the 5th, mean, median and 95th values, the MLE and the Beta marginal a and b, and converts mean alpha factors to MGL parameters. Many system-specific templates have zero CCF events and stay close to the prior. Two templates (ALL-PDP-FR and CCF-DEM) print summary tables that do not match their distribution tables.
sources.reference: Z. Ma and K. J. Kvarfordt, CCF Parameter Estimations, 2020 Update, INL/EXT-21-62940 Revision 1, Idaho National Laboratory, August 2022

entries.method: Beta marginal (printed a, b) of the Dirichlet posterior from the 2015 prior and 2006-2020 CCF data with 119.8 independent and 2 CCF events. Impact vector for CCCG 2: Adj. Ind 59.90, N1 1.5000, N2 0.2500 (failures = N2).

sources.name: SAND2022-14164 Compressed Natural Gas Component Leak Frequency Estimation
sources.covers: Annual leak frequency distributions for 11 CNG component types in five leak area bins, plus the literature leak frequencies behind them
sources.boundaryConvention: Components are binned by type only: compressor, filter, flange or gasket, heat exchanger, hose, instrument, joint, jumper, pipe, valve and vessel. Sizes and subtypes are pooled, so one valve estimate covers every valve. Leak size is the leak area as a fraction of the flow area of the connected piping, in bins of 0.01%, 0.1%, 1%, 10% and 100%.
sources.failureCounting: No events are counted. The inputs are published leak frequencies from a literature review, listed in Appendix A and mapped to leak area bins by qualitative labels or by area ratios. Only compressed gas data feed the model when they exist, and instruments and joints use generic data. The years shown are the publication years of the data sources.
sources.quality: A Bayesian log-linear model of log frequency against log leak area is fit by Markov chain Monte Carlo for each component. The compressed gas data are sparse and old, and none fall in the 0.01% and 0.1% bins, so those bins are extrapolated. The authors warn that the uncertainty may be underestimated and recommend the medians for QRA.
sources.reference: D. Brooks, A. Glover, B. D. Ehrhart, SAND2022-14164, Sandia National Laboratories, October 2022

sources.name: SAND2020-10828 Hydrogen Plant Hazards and Risk Analysis for Siting near Nuclear Power Plants
sources.covers: Generic and hydrogen component leak frequencies by leak size, facility leak frequency for a steam electrolysis hydrogen plant, and wind fragilities of nuclear plant structures and switchyard parts
sources.boundaryConvention: Leak frequencies are per component type with subtypes and sizes pooled. Leak size is the leak area as a fraction of the total flow area: very small 0.01%, minor 0.1%, medium 1%, major 10% and rupture 100%. Pipe frequencies are per meter of pipe. Fragilities are conditional failure probabilities of plant structures and switchyard parts at a given wind speed.
sources.failureCounting: Generic leak frequencies are published values from chemical process, compressed gas, nuclear and offshore sources (Table B-1), published from 1975 to 2007. Hydrogen leak counts over component-years come from Compressed Gas Association members through NFPA 2 TG6, cited from LaChance et al. (SAND2009-0874), and are not shown. Wind fragilities are taken from the Duane Arnold IPEEE and a Vogtle high wind study.
sources.quality: A Bayesian log-linear model of leak frequency against leak area is fit by Markov chain Monte Carlo to the generic data and then updated with the hydrogen counts. Generic data exist only for the 1%, 10% and 100% bins, so smaller bins are extrapolated. The facility frequency multiplies assumed component counts and pipe lengths for a postulated design.
sources.reference: A. Glover, A. Baird, D. Brooks, SAND2020-10828, Sandia National Laboratories, October 2020

sources.name: NUREG-1829, Estimating Loss-of-Coolant Accident (LOCA) Frequencies Through the Elicitation Process, Vols. 1 and 2
sources.covers: Expert elicitation LOCA frequencies for BWRs and PWRs by flow rate category and plant age, with sensitivity cases, plus base case pipe failure rates, LOCA frequencies and PFM probabilities.
sources.boundaryConvention: LOCA categories are cumulative flow rate thresholds from more than 100 gpm to more than 500,000 gpm, each with a BWR and a PWR effective break size. Only passive primary pressure boundary failures count, both piping and non-piping such as the vessel, nozzles, valve bodies, pump casings and steam generator tubes. Active failures such as stuck-open valves and pump seal LOCAs are excluded. Panelists used ASME rules to split piping from non-piping.
sources.failureCounting: No LOCA of Category 2 or larger has occurred, so the estimates rest on expert judgment anchored to base cases. The base cases use pipe failure records from about 1970 to 2003 (PIPExp, SLAP and LERs) and PFM codes. Category 1 checks use U.S. operating experience to December 2006. Frequencies are per calendar year unless a table states reactor years.
sources.quality: Twelve panelists gave median and 5th and 95th percentile ratios relative to the base cases. Responses were combined as split lognormals and aggregated with the geometric mean, with arithmetic-mean and mixture aggregation as sensitivity cases. Uncertainty is very large and the group results depend most on the aggregation method. The report does not recommend one set of estimates for all uses.
sources.reference: R. Tregoning, L. Abramson, P. Scott, NUREG-1829 Vols. 1 and 2, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, April 2008

sources.name: NUREG-1715 Component Performance Study, Vols. 1-4 (turbine-driven pumps, motor-driven pumps, air-operated valves, motor-operated valves)
sources.covers: Probability of failure on demand, standby failure rates, failures per component-year and failure cause shares for safety-related pumps and valves in U.S. light water reactors
sources.boundaryConvention: A turbine-driven pump assembly is the pump, turbine driver and governor with their piece parts. Steam inlet, suction and discharge valves, flow instruments and remote controls are outside. A motor-driven pump assembly is the pump, motor and circuit breaker. Valve assemblies are the valve body plus the air or motor operator, without MSIVs, PORVs, non-integral instrument air parts or the MOV circuit breaker.
sources.failureCounting: Only complete failures of Application Coded components in risk-important systems count. NPRDS gives surveillance test failures and test frequencies for 1987-1995, and LERs in SCSS give ESF actuation failures and demands for 1987-1998. Pump start and run failures and valve open, close and operate failures are pooled as failure on demand. Surveillance demands are estimated from test frequency, component count and years.
sources.quality: Failure on demand uses a Bayes method with a beta plant-to-plant distribution fit by maximum likelihood, or a noninformative prior for sparse data, with 90% intervals. Classical 90% chi-square intervals are given for information. Standby rates divide failures by calendar component-hours, so they are not run-time rates. The volumes are scanned and some printed values disagree between tables, which the affected entries note.
sources.reference: J. R. Houghton and H. G. Hamzehee (Vols. 1-2) and J. R. Houghton (Vols. 3-4), NUREG-1715 Vols. 1-4, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research, April 2000, June 2000, July 2001 and September 2001

sources.name: NUREG/CR-6890 Vols. 1 and 2 (INL/EXT-05-00501) with the LOOP 2023 update (INL/RPT-24-79969)
sources.covers: Loss of offsite power frequencies by category and plant mode, recovery time distributions and non-recovery probabilities, emergency diesel generator reliability and CCF factors, and station blackout core damage results
sources.boundaryConvention: A LOOP is the simultaneous loss of offsite power to all safety buses of a unit that requires all emergency generators to start. Events are split into plant-centered, switchyard-centered, grid-related and weather-related LOOPs, with the main and station transformer high-voltage terminals and the point where lines leave the switchyard as the borders. Critical operation counts LOOPs with a reactor trip, and shutdown operation counts LOOPs while the unit is shut down. EDG failure modes follow the SPAR models: fail to start, fail to load and run for 1 h, fail to run after 1 h, and test or maintenance unavailability.
sources.failureCounting: LOOP events come from licensee event reports and are counted per unit for frequencies. Durations use the potential bus recovery time, counted once per site when several units are hit by one event. LOOPs without a reactor trip and partial LOOPs are not counted. EDG counts come from EPIX for 1998-2002 and from unplanned undervoltage demands in LERs for 1997-2003.
sources.quality: Frequencies are Jeffreys or constrained noninformative Bayesian updates, or empirical Bayes gamma distributions where plant or site variation was found. Recovery times are lognormal fits by matching moments. SBO core damage values are SPAR model point estimates and Monte Carlo uncertainty results. Volumes 1 and 2 are scanned pages, so values were read from the OCR text and checked against page images and internal identities.
sources.reference: S. A. Eide, C. D. Gentillon, T. E. Wierman and D. M. Rasmuson, NUREG/CR-6890 Vols. 1 and 2 (INL/EXT-05-00501), U.S. NRC and Idaho National Laboratory, December 2005. N. Johnson and Z. Ma, Analysis of Loss-of-Offsite-Power Events 2023 Update, INL/RPT-24-79969, Idaho National Laboratory, July 2024.
